title: Job's Oath of Innocence
summary: Job ends his speeches with a solemn series of oaths. He denies lust, deceit, adultery, mistreating his servants, neglecting the poor, the widow, and the orphan, trusting in wealth, worshiping the sun and moon, gloating over his enemy, failing in hospitality, and hiding his sins. For many of these he calls down a curse on himself if he is guilty. In the middle he signs his defense and demands that the Almighty answer him. Then the words of Job are ended.
story: This is the climax of Job's final monologue (chapters 29 to 31) and of all his speeches. In chapter 29 he recalled his past honor; in chapter 30 he lamented his present humiliation. Now he makes his formal defense. Since chapter 9, Job has longed for a hearing before God; in chapter 13 he prepared his case; in chapter 23 he wished he knew where to find God. Here he finally submits it, signing it like a legal document and challenging God to respond. The narrator closes the chapter with the words, Thus conclude the words of Job. Everyone now waits for God. Instead, a young man named Elihu steps forward (chapters 32 to 37), and only after him does God answer from the whirlwind (chapter 38).
historical:
The chapter takes the form of an oath of clearance, a legal procedure known in the ancient Near East. When a person was accused and there was no evidence to settle the case, he could swear an oath before God, often with a self-curse: if I have done this, may such and such happen to me. Israel's law used oaths in this way (Exodus 22:10-11; Numbers 5:19-22). By swearing, the accused placed the case in God's hands. If he lied, God himself would bring the curse to pass.

There is also a well-known Egyptian parallel. Chapter 125 of the Egyptian Book of the Dead contains a declaration in which the dead person, standing before the gods in judgment, denies a long list of wrongs, such as stealing, lying, and doing harm to the poor. Job's oath has a similar form, but it differs in important ways: it is made by a living man, before the one God, and it focuses much more on the heart and on care for others.
cultural:
The chapter touches many areas of ancient life. Verse 10's curse, that his wife grind grain for another, pictures her reduced to slavery, since grinding grain at a hand mill was the daily work of servants and captives. Verses 13-15 concern household slaves, who in the ancient world had few rights; Job insists that he heard their complaints because the same God made them in the womb. Verse 21 refers to the city gate, where Job had support, meaning influence among the elders who decided cases.

Verses 26-27 describe the worship of the sun and moon, widespread throughout the ancient Near East. Throwing a kiss with the hand was a gesture of reverence toward a deity (compare 1 Kings 19:18, where kissing is linked with Baal worship). Job says that even this secret gesture would be a denial of God on high. Verse 32 reflects the ancient duty of hospitality, which required householders to take in travelers so they did not have to spend the night in the open street (compare Genesis 19:2 and Judges 19:15-21). Verse 35's signature translates the Hebrew letter tav, the last letter of the alphabet, which in the older script was written as a cross mark. Job is putting his mark on his statement like a signature on a legal document.
literary: The chapter is built from a series of if clauses, each denying a sin, several followed by a then clause calling down a punishment. The sins move from inner desire (the covenant with his eyes, verse 1) to outward acts, from private sins to public injustice, from the treatment of people to the worship of God, and finally to the land itself (verses 38-40). The effect is a comprehensive picture of a righteous life, stretching from the heart to the fields. Verses 35-37 interrupt the list with Job's climactic challenge, in which he signs his defense and dares God to write the charge against him. Many scholars think verses 38-40 originally came earlier and have been moved; others see them as a deliberate final flourish that brings the whole oath back to the land and to God's creation. The narrator's closing note (verse 40) marks the end of Job's words until his brief replies to God in chapters 40 and 42.

outline.t: Servants, the poor, the widow, and the orphan
Trust in gold and worship of the sun and moon
Here is my signature: let the Almighty answer me
The land, and the end of Job's words

doctrines.note: Job's oath covers much of what Israel's law requires, but it goes beyond outward acts to the heart: lust in the eyes, secret trust in gold, private worship of the sun, and gloating over an enemy. It anticipates the teaching of Jesus that righteousness is a matter of the heart.

Job grounds his fair treatment of his slaves in creation: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them?” (verse 15). This is one of the clearest statements in the Old Testament of the equal dignity of all people before God.

Job names trust in gold and worship of the sun and moon as twin forms of idolatry and calls both a denial of God on high (verse 28). Idolatry can be as private as a kiss blown to the moon or as ordinary as confidence in wealth.

words.note: Berit, covenant. It is the word used for God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel, and David, and for binding agreements between people. In verse 1 Job says he made a covenant with his eyes, a solemn commitment not to look at a woman with desire. He applies covenant language to the discipline of his own heart.

Tummah, integrity. In verse 6 Job asks God to weigh him with honest scales so that God may know his integrity. The word returns from the prologue (2:3, 9) and from Job's oath in 27:5. The whole book turns on whether it is real.

Tav, a mark, the name of the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In the older Hebrew script it was shaped like an X or a cross. In verse 35 the BSB renders it signature: Job puts his mark on his defense. The same word is used in Ezekiel 9:4 for the mark put on the foreheads of the faithful.

Adam, the name of the first man, and also the ordinary Hebrew word for human being. In verse 33 Job says he has not covered his sins like Adam, which may refer to Adam hiding from God in Genesis 3 or may simply mean as people do. Both readings are possible and are reflected in translations.

christ: Job's oath anticipates the heart-level righteousness Jesus taught. Job made a covenant with his eyes not to look at a virgin with desire; Jesus taught that looking at a woman with lust is already adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:28). Job refused to rejoice over his enemy's ruin; Jesus taught his followers to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44). Job's care for the poor, the widow, the orphan, and the stranger is the same care Jesus names in his parable of the sheep and goats (Matthew 25:35-36), where feeding the hungry, welcoming the stranger, and clothing the naked are done for Christ himself. Job presented his righteousness and asked God to answer; the New Testament presents Jesus as the one who was truly without sin (Hebrews 4:15) and who offered his righteousness not in his own defense but on behalf of others. The link is thematic. Job's oath shows how high the standard is, and the gospel shows who met it.

hard.q: Is Job claiming to be sinless?
hard.a: Job's oath covers an astonishing range of possible sins, and it can sound like a claim to moral perfection. But Job has elsewhere acknowledged that no one is pure before God (9:2; 14:4), and he speaks of the sins of his youth (13:26). His oath is not a claim to sinlessness in general but a denial of the specific kinds of wrongdoing that would justify his disaster, the kind of guilt the friends insist he must have. In verse 33 he even implies that he has sins, since the point is that he has not hidden them. Many interpreters also note that Job's standard is extraordinarily high, reaching to his eyes and heart, which is the opposite of self-righteous minimalism. At the same time, the book will show that Job's confidence in his own righteousness led him to speak as if God owed him an explanation, and God will challenge that (40:8). Job is innocent of the charges, as God himself says, but he is not beyond correction.

questions: Job made a covenant with his eyes. What would it look like for you to make a commitment like that in an area of temptation?
Job says that the same God made him and his slaves in the womb (verse 15). How should that truth shape the way you treat people who work for you or depend on you?
Job signs his defense and demands that God answer. What do you want to ask God, and how do you think he might answer?
